payload.title: Fix regex queries for multi-value fields

payload.author: copilot-pull-request-reviewer
payload.body:
## Pull request overview grug see PR fix regex query on multi-value field (DelimitedString) so fast SQL path match each stored value, not whole serialized blob. this make `genres::^Electro$` hit `Electro` but not `Electroclash`, like python slow path. **Changes:** - teach `Item.field_query()` to pass DelimitedString DB delimiter into `RegexpQuery` when using regex - extend `RegexpQuery` SQL clause + sqlite `regexp()` function to accept optional delimiter and test each split value - add regression test + changelog entry for :bug:`6961` ### Reviewed changes Copilot reviewed 5 out of 5 changed files in this pull request and generated 1 comment.
Show a summary per file | File | Description | | ---- | ----------- | | test/dbcore/test_query.py | add regression test for regex matching single value in multi-value field on fast path | | docs/changelog.rst | document bug fix for multi-valued regex query semantics | | beets/library/models.py | pass DelimitedString db delimiter when building RegexpQuery | | beets/dbcore/query.py | add optional delimiter param and emit 3-arg `regexp()` SQL call | | beets/dbcore/db.py | register 3-arg sqlite `regexp()` and split multi-value strings before matching |

payload.title: edit: Keep rejected album fields visible per track

payload.author: copilot-pull-request-reviewer
payload.body: ## Pull request overview This PR fix edit plugin import flow. Before, grug see item-only fields (like `title`, `track`) get rejected from album header, but then also disappear from per-track docs when user use `edit Candidates`. Now only fields that actually land in album header get removed from track docs, so rejected header fields still show per-track when in `itemfields`. **Changes:** - In `beetsplug/edit.py`, compute track-field exclusion from the *built* album header keys (not raw `albumfields` config). - Add regression test for `edit Candidates` flow to prove rejected header fields stay editable per-track. - Update edit plugin docs + changelog entry for behavior change. ### Reviewed changes Copilot reviewed 4 out of 4 changed files in this pull request and generated no comments. | File | Description | | ---- | ----------- | | beetsplug/edit.py | Track doc field set now excludes only fields actually present in album header. | | test/plugins/test_edit.py | New regression test covering `edit Candidates` with overlapping `albumfields`/`itemfields`. | | docs/plugins/edit.rst | Docs now describe “accepted into header” vs “rejected stays per-track” behavior. | | docs/changelog.rst | Add bugfix note for :bug:`6953`. | --- 💡 Add a `code-review` agent skill or configure MCP servers for context-aware, tailored reviews. payload.author: copilot-pull-request-reviewer

## Pull request overview grug see PR make issue/PR labeler smarter about beets CLI words in title. grug like goal: triage faster, reviewer route easier. **Changes:** - add extra regex for many plugins to match “X command” and “beet X” title text - add new “Commands” label section for core `beet` commands (`config`, `import`, `list`, `modify`, `update`, etc.)
Suppressed comments (1) **.github/labeler.yaml:37** * grug see `bpm:` label no match `bpm plugin` / `bpm:` text, only `bpm command` or `beet bpm`. grug think add safe plugin-name pattern (with `plugin|:`) so titles about plugin still label, but not match random "120 bpm" talk. ``` bpm: - '/bpm command/i' - '/beet bpm/i' ```

* grug read PR text say `beets.dbcore.sort` accept `Iterable` now. but code change use `Sequence`, still reject many iterables (like iterators / generator / Results) for typing. if goal is accept any iterable, need swap `Sequence` -> `Iterable` (and update overrides in this file same way so signatures match).

    def sort(self, items: Sequence[AnyModel]) -> Sequence[AnyModel]:

```

* grug see test call `ipfs_play(self.lib, None, [])` but new typing say `opts: optparse.Values`. if mypy check tests, this fail. pass real optparse.Values (can grab from beetsplug.ipfs module) so test match command interface.

<details>

**beets/ui/__init__.py:475**
* grug see add_album_option now set default=False. this break config mirror trick. many plugin do `self.config.set_args(opts)` and have `album` in config (ex duplicates plugin). if user set `duplicates: album: yes` and run `beet duplicates` with no `-a`, opts.album False will override config back to False, so config no work (docs say config options mirror CLI). better keep album default None so set_args can skip when user not pass flag, and call sites can use `bool(opts.album)` when they need strict bool.
```
        album = optparse.Option(
            *flags,
            action="store_true",
            default=False,
            help="match albums instead of tracks",
        )
```

payload.author: henry-oberholtzer
payload.body:
The code for this PR looks good to me! I think my question is whether immediately retrying a query immediately after a failure seems to actually yield results after a json.decode() error.

If it's an outage on the discogs server side, my instinct is that it won't fix it, but I could be totally wrong if anyone has anecdotal experience with this issue.

It's also hard to test if a re-search actuallr recovers errors from discogs since it seems to be a white whale issue - none of this is to say we shouldn't try to give a query another shot in a failure.

EDIT:

Well, anecdotally - it seems to resolve it according to this post: https://github.com/joalla/discogs_client/issues/163#issuecomment-3403116431

payload.author: treyturner
payload.body:
> It's also hard to test if a re-search actually recovers errors

My anecdotal experience is also that a retry returns success, but that's usually after at least a few seconds following an abort and restart of the current import. We may find success to be less likely when immediately retried. I added a log line indicating the retry so that we can later evaluate if a small sleep between attempts may increase the chance of success.

payload.author: treyturner
payload.body:
> This seems like something to me that could be part of the `discogs_client` instead.

I can definitely appreciate this take. I considered that approach as well, but given the discussion and apparent ambiguity in https://github.com/joalla/discogs_client/issues/163, I thought this one small effort upstream could protect the user experience while `discogs_client` continues working through opportunities to improve consistency. If it required really anything else here in `beets` I'd not have been comfortable proposing it.

Still, I completely understand if this is desired downstream instead. Thanks for your consideration!

payload.author: JOJ0
payload.body:
> This seems like something to me that could be part of the `discogs_client` instead. @JOJ0 Assigning you here since this seems to be right in your expertise 🙃

Not any time soon doesn't mean _never_ :-) It is out of scope to discuss this here in the beets project, I want to do it anyway since now we sit together around the camp fire and talk about it already ;-) No, seriously I was thinking about catching this error originally as the linked discussion in the upstream project suggests. I am still not sure what to do with a catch then. If we do nothing (return None?) we might run into errors elsewhere.

So I figure we must do something about it: Should we retry it once like in this PR here? That might work or might not work and doesnt really sound like a solution that will always make sense.

Should we implement some "back off for a random time and try later approach" and then do that a configurable amount of times? (similar to what rate limiting handlers do)

Are we doing the right thing already? We notify the caller that there is a serious error and they need to handle it themselves: We throw an exception. Well, the exception could tell something more useful like: _There is a serious error happening on discogs.com, probably somewhere in their backend_ - but that is heavy guesswork also and not much better, and probably just wrong.

What's your suggestions discogs_client should do when it hits such an error?

What do other libraries do when their backend has an error? Don't they just throw an exception since it is a non-predictable non-recoverable error?

And by the way, whenever I experienced these errors ,of course this website doesnt show any discogs outage 🤣 https://github.com/joalla/discogs_client/issues/163#issuecomment-2676848514

payload.author: semohr
payload.body:
> What do other libraries do when their backend has an error? Don't they just throw an exception since it is a non-predictable non-recoverable error?

If it is truely unpredictable there is nothing one can do as api wrapper developer really.

Generally what I would like tho, is an obvious error. We can than catch it here and handle approprietly, just relying on a json decode exception seems a bit strange and messy imo. Something like a generic `DiscogsbackendError` could work. Here in beets we can than handle that error and retry once or with backoff if appropriate.

HI @semohr, thanks so much for you opinion. Much appreciated. I agree that a "definitive error" would be a good middleground here. Since we don't _really_ know what the origin of the error is I'd word this even more general and try not to guess what or _where_ this is/was happening. We don't really know what "in the backend" means, so.... What we know is that it is not a regular result so maybe something like `DiscogsMalformedResponseError" or even `DiscogsUnexpectedError`. Anyway thanks again I'll redirect this now to the upstream project.

payload.author: semohr
payload.body:
I would keep the non-regex version. The logic here is straightforward, and I don't think it's worth compiling four regex patterns just because we import the Tidal plugin.

For example, to understand this:

```python
partial(
    re.compile(r"^(?:(?:©|℗|\([cp]\)) *)?(?:\d{4} )?", re.IGNORECASE).sub, ""
)
```

a reader needs to:

- understand the regex itself,
- know what re.compile() is doing,
- and know why functools.partial() is being used.

That's a fair amount of indirection for logic that is otherwise very simple.

The explicit version:

```python
for marker in ("©", "℗", "(C)", "(P)", "(c)", "(p)"):
    if text.startswith(marker):
        text = text[len(marker):].strip()
        break

```
is immediately obvious to most Python developers, even those who aren't comfortable with regexes. It also avoids the overhead of compiling regex patterns, so it's slightly more efficient as well.

Unless the matching logic becomes substantially more complex, I'd favor the simpler, more explicit implementation.


---

If we combine all patterns into a **single compiled regex**, the performance argument becomes less relevant. 

For me, the stronger argument remains that the explicit implementation communicates the intent more clearly. Unless the matching rules become substantially more complex, I would favor the simpler, more direct approach.

---

Regarding this topic, I recommend  https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1109/ASE.2019.00047

payload.author: snejus
payload.body:
> I would keep the non-regex version. The logic here is straightforward, and I don't think it's worth compiling four regex patterns just because we import the Tidal plugin.
> 
> For example, to understand this:
> 
> ```python
> partial(
>     re.compile(r"^(?:(?:©|℗|\([cp]\)) *)?(?:\d{4} )?", re.IGNORECASE).sub, ""
> )
> ```
> 
> a reader needs to:
> 
>     * understand the regex itself,
> 
>     * know what re.compile() is doing,
> 
>     * and know why functools.partial() is being used.
> 
> 
> That's a fair amount of indirection for logic that is otherwise very simple.
> 
> The explicit version:
> 
> ```python
> for marker in ("©", "℗", "(C)", "(P)", "(c)", "(p)"):
>     if text.startswith(marker):
>         text = text[len(marker):].strip()
>         break
> ```
> 
> is immediately obvious to most Python developers, even those who aren't comfortable with regexes. It also avoids the overhead of compiling regex patterns, so it's slightly more efficient as well.
> 
> Unless the matching logic becomes substantially more complex, I'd favor the simpler, more explicit implementation.
> 
> If we combine all patterns into a **single compiled regex**, the performance argument becomes less relevant.
> 
> For me, the stronger argument remains that the explicit implementation communicates the intent more clearly. Unless the matching rules become substantially more complex, I would favor the simpler, more direct approach.
> 
> Regarding this topic, I recommend https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1109/ASE.2019.00047

Thanks for expanding on this. I agree that the previous combined `_remove_leading` expression was unnecessarily dense, so I'd suggest to split it into independently named `_remove_copyright` and `_remove_year` transformations:

```py
_remove_copyright = partial(
    re.compile(r"^(©|℗|\([cp]\)) *", re.IGNORECASE).sub, ""
)
_remove_year = partial(re.compile(r"^\d{4} ", re.IGNORECASE).sub, "")
```

With that change, I find the complete regex version easier to follow than the string version. The normalization policy is visible as one short pipeline:

```python
[
    _remove_copyright,
    _remove_year,
    _remove_license,
    _remove_trailing_clause,
    _remove_legal_suffix,
]
```

Each regex now has one narrowly named responsibility. They also use only basic regex features that developers should be familiar with. By comparison, the string version spreads the same policy across repeated `lower()`, loops, `index()`, slicing, temporary phrase variables, and roughly 40 lines of control flow. The isolated marker loop is straightforward, but it is only one part of the full comparison. As a maintainer, I find 5 simple regexes much easier to maintain than a long function with custom string-method-based replacement logic.

`partial(re.compile(...).sub, "")` is also an existing pattern in the lyrics plugin, and `apply_transforms` is now shared by both callers, so this is not a new local convention.

I don't think performance should decide this either way. `_normalize_label()` runs once per candidate, and both implementations complete in under 100 μs. At that call frequency and absolute cost, any difference between them is immaterial, so I think we should choose based on readability. The regexes are also compiled once rather than once per candidate.

I read the paper you linked. It supports caution around complex regexes, but it also reports that developers choose regexes for medium-complexity matching and prefer shorter expressions with fewer features. I think these small, named, tested transformations fit that use case better than one large imperative function.

payload.author: semohr
payload.body:
To keep this brief, I see it differently. For this transformation, I find a few explicit string operations easier to read and maintain than **five separate** regular expressions. Each operation describes exactly what it removes or changes, while the equivalent regexes require readers to decode the patterns.

I’m fine with either of these approaches:

a) Use small string-method helpers, optionally through the existing `apply_transforms` pipeline.
b) Use a single regex to parse the complete label. This is more concise, but concentrates more complexity into one pattern.

As a maintainer and the code owner of the tidal plugin, I’m happy to maintain either solution. Beets already uses regex-based transformation rules in some plugin APIs, so I’m not opposed to regex in principle, I just don’t think it is the clearest choice here, since these transformations are simple and sequential rather than pattern-heavy. The relevant formats and edge cases should be covered by tests either way.

payload.author: snejus
payload.body:
Thanks. I understand what both alternatives would look like mechanically, but I don't yet understand how either would improve readability over the current design. Could you compare each option against the current implementation as a whole?

For option (a), we would keep the named transformation pipeline but replace each short regex with a custom helper containing some combination of loops, `lower()`, `index()`, slicing, suffix lists, and temporary variables. The individual string operations are familiar, but the complete implementation is substantially longer and spreads each matching rule across more control flow. What makes that easier to read or maintain than the current small, named regex transformations?

For example, I find 
```py
_remove_license = partial(
    re.compile(r".* under exclusive licence to ", re.IGNORECASE).sub, ""
)
```
more readable than
```py
        # "under exclusive license to"
        phrase = "under exclusive license to"
        phrase_alt = "under exclusive licence to"

        lower = text.lower()
        for p in (phrase, phrase_alt):
            if p in lower:
                idx = lower.index(p)
                text = text[idx + len(p) :]
                break
```

For option (b), the transformations do different things: some remove a prefix, one keeps the text after a phrase, and others keep the text before a phrase or remove a suffix. Combining those behaviors into one regex appears to require optional branches, capture groups, and conditional replacement logic. That seems considerably harder to understand than keeping one basic regex per named rule.

The current design keeps the policy visible in one place:

```python
[
    _remove_copyright,
    _remove_year,
    _remove_license,
    _remove_trailing_clause,
    _remove_legal_suffix,
]
```

Each transformation has one responsibility and uses only basic regex features. Setting performance aside, could you explain which specific part of this design remains less readable, and how either (a) or (b) improves that aspect? I'm not arguing that regex is always preferable. I'm trying to understand why the middle option of several small, named regex transformations is being excluded.

payload.author: semohr
payload.body:
The argument I am making (and the point discussed in the paper) is that, since these individual transformations are very simple, introducing regex does not necessarily improve readability. If we consider the complete transformation as one operation, a single, explicit implementation of the transformation logic may be easier to understand than a sequence of separate regex-based rules.

For option (a), I am not primarily arguing that the helper functions are more readable line by line. My point is more about the effort required to understand what is actually happening to the string. With the multi regex implementation, the reader has to interpret several independent regex patterns and mentally reconstruct their combined effect. A direct implementation makes the string manipulation steps explicit, even if it requires more lines of code.

For option (b), I think I did not explain the intention clearly enough. The goal is not to introduce a more complex regex-based solution, but rather to reduce the current boilerplate around the transformations. The idea is to describe the complete transformation in one place and keep the implementation concise.

```python
re.compile(
    r"^(?:(?:©|℗|\([cp]\))\s*)?"          # optional copyright / phonogram marker
    r"(?:\d{4}\s+)?"                      # optional year
    r"(?:.*? under exclusive licen[sc]e to )?"  # optional license prefix
    r"(.*?)"                              # text to keep
    r"(?:, (?:a|for the united states and) .*"  # optional trailing clause
    r"|,? (?:inc|llc|ltd|co)\.?)?$",      # optional legal suffix
    re.IGNORECASE,
)
```
The advantage of option (b) is not adding another abstraction layer, but removing unnecessary repetition while keeping the transformation logic in one place.

---

In summary, option (a) favors transparency and step-by-step explainability, whereas option (b) favors simplicity and a more compact implementation.

>     re.IGNORECASE,
> )
> ```

I think I'd be happy with this, provided that we use a single string with `re.VERBOSE` flag.

Avoided the walrus form because a flex value can legitimately be None and `.get(...) is not None` would treat it as missing.

payload.author: davidbhoward
payload.title: lyrics: don't match LRCLib entries that have no lyrics

payload.author: davidbhoward
payload.body:
Full disclosure on where this came from: I have not personally reviewed the code in this
PR. Claude found the issue while backfilling lyrics across my music library and wrote the
fix and the tests. What I hit was imports aborting partway through on instrumental lo-fi
tracks, which left the rest of the batch sitting unimported without any obvious error.

The repro in the description is a real response from the LRCLib API, so at minimum the
underlying behavior is worth knowing about even if you want to solve it differently.

Posting it in case it helps. Take it or leave it, no hard feelings either way.

payload.author: davidbhoward
payload.body:
The two failures in the ubuntu 3.10 job look unrelated to this change. I reverted
beetsplug/lyrics.py and _typing.py to master locally and ran the same two tests, and
they fail identically without my change.

Both are live network tests in TestLyricsSources. The lyricsmania one is the Google
backend, which this PR does not touch at all. The lrclib one has matching lyrics text
and only differs on the record URL, 23863037 versus the expected 19648857, so it looks
like LRCLib is serving a different record ID for the same song now.

These only run when lyrics source changes, so I think this PR just happened to be what
made them run.

payload.author: semohr
payload.body:
Is this still an issue on the master branch?

I think https://github.com/beetbox/beets/pull/6864/ should have fixed this already.

payload.author: davidbhoward
payload.body:
> Is this still an issue on the master branch?
> 
> I think #6864 should have fixed this already.

Thanks for pointing at #6864. I checked and I don't think it covers this one: #6864 is
already in master (77b9dffc4) and the crash still reproduces on it.

The difference is where the None comes from. #6864 guards Lyrics.from_item(), which handles
item.lyrics being None for a track with no stored lyrics. This crash never goes through
from_item. LRCLib.fetch() builds the Lyrics object directly:

    lyrics = item.get_text(self.config["synced"].get(bool))   # returns None
    return Lyrics(lyrics, self.__class__.name, ...)

get_text() falls through to `return self.plain`, and plainLyrics is null in the API response
even though instrumental is false, so None reaches the constructor rather than from_item.

The repro in the PR description is a real LRCLib response and it still fails on current
master. Happy to be wrong if I've misread something.

payload.author: semohr
payload.body: Thanks for the clarification! Makes sense to me.

payload.author: snejus
payload.body: @davidbhoward I fixed `lrclib` integration test as it failed. Please address my comment and we will merge it :)

payload.author: davidbhoward
payload.body: OK will do. I'm on vacation but will do it when I get back next week. Thank you.

payload.author: davidbhoward
payload.body:
Both review points are addressed in f68aefa.

I also rebased onto current master rather than merging, so the earlier commit SHAs changed.
Your lrclib fixture fix is still there as b19f0c0 with your authorship, I cherry-picked it onto
the rebase so it did not get lost. Both TestLyricsSources live tests pass locally now.

I wasn't sure if this project prefers rebase or merging master into branch.  Let me know if you need to take any action here. Sorry about that.

payload.author: davidbhoward
payload.body:
CI is red on ubuntu 3.10 again but it looks like more provider drift rather than anything
from this change.

The failure is now TestLyricsSources[lrcmux-lrcmux]:

    FAILED test/plugins/test_lyrics.py::TestLyricsSources::test_backend_source[lrcmux-lrcmux]
    AssertionError: assert '[00:00.00]\n...ake ends meet' == '[00:08.71] L...ake ends meet'

The only difference is a leading empty timestamp line that ytmusic has started returning. Every
other line matches exactly:

    + [00:00.00]
      [00:08.71] Lady Madonna, children at your feet
      [00:13.08] Wonder how you manage to make ends meet
      [00:17.43] Who finds the money when you pay the rent?
      ...

Reasons I do not think it is this PR:

I reverted beetsplug/lyrics.py and beetsplug/_typing.py to origin/master locally and the test
fails identically, so it reproduces without any of my changes.

This PR does not touch that fixture. The only change to lyrics_pages.py on this branch is your
lrclib URL fix.

The change itself cannot add a line. _synced_as_plain only removes timestamps and
_format_synced only trims whitespace on existing lines.

For what it is worth this is the third live source to drift on this PR now, first lyricsmania,
then the lrclib record ID you fixed, now ytmusic. Since these only run when lyrics source files
change, the drift seems to pile up and then land on whoever next touches the plugin.

Happy to add the leading [00:00.00] to the expected text in this PR if you want it fixed here,
or leave it for a separate one. Let me know which you prefer.

payload.title: lastgenre: Album stage fall back to multi-valued albumartists

payload.author: copilot-pull-request-reviewer
payload.body:
## Pull request overview

PR make `lastgenre` album stage smarter for multi-artist albums. When Last.fm give no album tags for main `albumartist`, plugin now try album lookup for each value in multi-valued `albumartists`, then still fall through to artist stage if nothing found.

**Changes:**
- Add `_try_resolve_album_stage` helper to hold album-stage logic and multi-valued `albumartists` fallback.
- Add focused unit test that exercises per-albumartist album lookup fallback.
- Document new multi-artist album behavior in `lastgenre` docs.

### Reviewed changes

Copilot reviewed 3 out of 3 changed files in this pull request and generated 2 comments.

| File | Description |
| ---- | ----------- |
| `beetsplug/lastgenre/__init__.py` | Add album-stage helper that falls back to per-`albumartists` album lookups when primary album lookup empty. |
| `test/plugins/test_lastgenre.py` | Add direct test for `_try_resolve_album_stage` fallback behavior. |
| `docs/plugins/lastgenre.rst` | Document album-stage fallback to multi-valued `albumartists` before artist source. |

payload.title: lastgenre: Improve original fallback (better use of aliases and count)

payload.author: copilot-pull-request-reviewer
payload.body:
## Pull request overview

PR make `lastgenre` original-genre fallback better when `force + keep_existing + whitelist (+ canonical)` is on. Goal is: do alias normalize + whitelist check without `_resolve_genres` path that can apply `count` too early, then only do canonical-parent fallback as last resort.

**Changes:**
- Change “original fallback” stage to alias-normalize originals, then run whitelist/ignore filtering directly (no `_try_resolve_stage` yet).
- Keep existing canonicalized-parent fallback via `_try_resolve_stage(...)` when nothing survives whitelist after aliasing.
- Update docstring to describe new fallback order.

payload.body:
Btw I created these two shell functions to add types to these event handlers 😁 

```zsh
python_add_type_checking() {
  # args: <import> [<file>, ...]
  # info: add type checking imports to Python files
  local import=${1:?<import> is missing} import_location import_token
  local -a files=(${${@:2}:?<file> is missing})
  import_token=${import##* import }
  import_location=${import% $import_token}
  local existing_import_pat='(^|\n *)'"$import_location"'[^\n]*'"$import_token"''

  isort --profile black -a 'from __future__ import annotations' $files
  isort --profile black -a 'from typing import TYPE_CHECKING' $files
  sed -z '
    # Add import if not already present
    /'"$existing_import_pat"'/!s/\n(from|import) .*\nif TYPE_CHECKING:\n/&    '"$import"'\n\n\n/
    # Add TYPE_CHECKING block if not already present and handle multiple imports
    /('"$existing_import_pat"'|\nif TYPE_CHECKING:\n)/!s/.*\n(from|import) ([^\n]+\n|[^(]+\(\n[^)]+\))\n/&if TYPE_CHECKING:\n    '"$import"'\n\n\n/
  ' -i $files
  format $files >/dev/null
  lint --select=I --fix $files >/dev/null
}

beets_type_event_handlers() {
  # args:
  # info: add types to event handler functions in beets
  msg "Adding type hints to beets event handlers"
  local -A mapping=(
    album       Album
    data        'Mapping[str, Any]'
    dest        bytes
    destination bytes
    info        AlbumInfo
    info        TrackInfo
    item        Item
    keepnew     bool
    lib         Library
    match       AlbumMatch
    model       LibModel
    path        bytes
    paths       'list[bytes]'
    session     ImportSession
    source      bytes
    tags        'dict[str, Any]'
    task        ImportTask
  )
  local pat
  local -a exprs files_and_funcs lines _files
  for _k _v in ${(kv)mapping}; exprs+=("s/(${_k})([,=)])/\1: ${_v}\2/")
  local pat="${(j:; :)exprs}; { / -> /!s/:$/ -> None:/; }"
  files_and_funcs=(${(f@)"$(
    oneline_python -H beets*/**/*.py |
    grep -P '(?<!def )register(_listener)?' |
    sed '
    /(self.register_listener|register)\(/!d
      s/^([^:]+)[^,]+, (self.)?([^)]+).*/\1: *def \3\\b/
    '
  )"})
  for _line in ${(f@)"$(
    sed '
      s/([^:]+):(.*)/sed -i ''\/^\2\/{$pat; }'' \1/
    ' <<<${(F)files_and_funcs}
  )"}; do
    eval ${(e)_line}
  done

  msg "Adding type checking imports for beets event handler types"
  local -A location_by_object=(
    Album         beets.library
    Item          beets.library
    Library       beets.library
    LibModel      beets.library
    AlbumInfo     beets.autotag
    AlbumMatch    beets.autotag
    TrackInfo     beets.autotag
    ImportSession beets.importer
    ImportTask    beets.importer
  )
  git add -u
  for _obj _loc in ${(kv)location_by_object}; do
    _files=($(git diff --staged -G $_obj --name-only))
    if (( $#_files )); then
      python_add_type_checking "from ${_loc} import ${_obj}" $_files
    fi
  done
  git add -u

  msg "Adding return type hints to plugin __init__ methods so that they are type checked"
  # get _files now because oneline_python_replace modifies staged files
  _files=($(git diff --staged --name-only))
  oneline_python_replace '(def __init__.*\)):$' '\1 -> None:'
  git add $_files
  git restore .

  warning "Untyped event handlers"
  _files=(${files_and_funcs%%:*})
  oneline_python -H $_files |
    grep -f =(print -l ${files_and_funcs//\\b}) |
    sort -u |
    grep -E ', [a-z0-9]+\b[,)=]'
}
```

`oneline_python` __unformats__ Python files where multi-line method definitions are unformatted into a single line, and `oneline_python_replace` does replacements. I've been using them for a long time.

payload.author: Sanjays2402
payload.title: fix: do not delete .mp3 file remuxed from MPEGLAYER3 WAV

payload.author: copilot-pull-request-reviewer
payload.body:
## Pull request overview

PR fix nasty bug in importer remux path. when WAV-with-MP3-stream file already end in `.mp3`, code write new bytes then delete same file. PR make delete only happen when output path not same as input. also add regression test + changelog note.

**Changes:**
- Guard `util.remove()` so remux-in-place (`.mp3` already) not delete output file
- Add test case for MPEGLAYER3 WAV stored with `.mp3` extension
- Document fix in changelog (bug #6748)

### Reviewed changes

Copilot reviewed 3 out of 3 changed files in this pull request and generated 3 comments.

| File | Description |
| ---- | ----------- |
| beets/util/extension.py | Avoid deleting remuxed output when input and output path are same |
| test/test_importer.py | Add regression test for `.mp3`-extension MPEGLAYER3 WAV case |
| docs/changelog.rst | Note bugfix in user-visible changelog |

payload.author: Sanjays2402
payload.body:
Applied all three. 8cf0e87.

The `!=` guard was genuinely wrong on a case-insensitive filesystem: with a `mpeglayer3.MP3` source, `with_suffix(".mp3")` produces a different `Path`, so the extracted stream was written over the same file and then `util.remove` deleted it. Now uses `util.samefile()`, which falls back to `os.path.samefile` and catches that.

Added `test_remux_mpeglayer3_wav_mp3_extension_uppercase` for it — it fails on the previous commit (`.MP3` gone after the call) and passes now. `pytest test/test_importer.py -k Mpeglayer` is 4 passed on macOS; note the uppercase case can only fail on a case-insensitive volume, so on a case-sensitive CI runner it passes either way.

Changelog and test docstring reworded to "has an `.mp3` extension".

## Pull request overview

PR move big chunk of test suite from mixed bytes/str paths toward `pathlib.Path`, so tests use one path model and prefer `item.filepath` / `album.art_filepath`. grug like less path soup, but grug see few spots where test logic break or helper removal break other tests.

**Changes:**
- Update many tests to build paths with `Path` ops, and use higher-level `filepath`/`art_filepath` APIs.
- Update test helper(s) to return `Path` (not bytes) for media fixtures; remove some old “touch” helpers.
- Small prod util tweak: `beets.util.mkdirall` now accepts `Path`.

### Reviewed changes

Copilot reviewed 36 out of 36 changed files in this pull request and generated 5 comments.

<details>

| File | Description |

| test/testall.py | Remove old path-hacking test runner helper. |
| test/test_util.py | Use `Path` for path construction in syspath tests. |
| test/test_library.py | Use `Path` in a few path-oriented tests; switch to `filepath.parent`, etc. |
| test/test_importer.py | Use `Path.mkdir()` / `Path.write_bytes()` in importer tests. |
| test/test_files.py | Migrate many filesystem ops to `Path` methods and `filepath`/`art_filepath`. |
| test/rsrc/convert_stub.py | Use `Path.open()` and `os.fsencode` for tag bytes. |
| test/plugins/test_web.py | Try to migrate stored Item/Album paths to `Path` and simplify expected strings. |
| test/plugins/test_thumbnails.py | Use `temp_path` and `Path.read_text()` for dolphin `.directory` check. |
| test/plugins/test_smartplaylist.py | Use `Path.unlink()` for playlist cleanup. |
| test/plugins/test_scrub.py | Pass `item.filepath` into `MediaFile`. |
| test/plugins/test_ipfs.py | Build expected IPFS paths with `Path` and compare via `filepath`. |
| test/plugins/test_info.py | Pass CLI file args as `str(Path)`; assert output includes decoded path. |
| test/plugins/test_importsource.py | Use `Path.stat()` for mtime checks. |
| test/plugins/test_importfeeds.py | Build configured playlist names/paths via `Path`. |
| test/plugins/test_importadded.py | Type annotate helper, use `Path.stat()` / `filepath` in assertions. |
| test/plugins/test_hook.py | Use `Path(...).is_file()` for file existence assertion. |
| test/plugins/test_filefilter.py | Compare expected item paths using `Item.filepath`. |
| test/plugins/test_fetchart.py | Use `album.filepath` / `album.art_filepath` and `Path.write_text()` in tests. |
| test/plugins/test_embedart.py | Use `Path` temp files + `Path.read_bytes()`; use `item.filepath.stat()` for mtimes. |
| test/plugins/test_duplicates.py | Assert output contains `str(item.filepath)` instead of `item.path.decode()`. |
| test/plugins/test_convert.py | Use `Path.write_text()` / `Path.read_text()` for converted file check. |

payload.author: TowyTowy
payload.body:
Good call, that's much nicer than erroring out. Reworked it so a reversed range just swaps its endpoints — `added:2024..2020` now means the same as `added:2020..2024`.

The swap happens in `from_periods` rather than `DateInterval.__init__`, since by the time `__init__` sees datetimes the endpoints have already been derived asymmetrically (start uses the period's date, end its open right endpoint), so swapping there gives the wrong interval. It also only kicks in when the range would otherwise be empty, so something like `2000-06..2000` still behaves as it does today.

payload.author: snejus
payload.body: What sort of negative consequences does this bug have?

payload.author: chuenchen309
payload.body:
Display-only — no data is touched — but it makes the import prompt show a string that isn't the candidate.

`colordiff()` produces multiple spans within one word whenever a correction touches two non-adjacent characters, which is exactly the common typo case. Against current master:

```python
from beets.util.diff import colordiff
from beets.util.color import uncolorize
from beets.util.layout import split_into_lines

left, right = colordiff("Extraordinary", "Extrabordinory")
# right == 'Extra\x1b[1;32mb\x1b[39;49;00mordin\x1b[1;32mo\x1b[39;49;00mry'

[uncolorize(l) for l in split_into_lines(right, 100, 100)]
# master: ['Extrabordin ory']   <- spurious space inside the word
# fix:    ['Extrabordinory']
```

So at the point where you're deciding whether to accept a match, the candidate renders as `Extrabordin ory` rather than `Extrabordinory`. The more highlighted spans a word has, the more spurious spaces appear.

It also mis-wraps: at width 12 master breaks after `Extrabordin` (11 chars) because it thinks the word ended there, while the fixed version fills the line properly (`Extrabordino` / `ry`).

Only reachable when the wrapping path runs (`beet import` diff output past terminal width), so it's cosmetic in severity — I'm happy to drop it if you'd rather not carry the extra state tracking for a display-only issue.

payload.author: Serene-Arc
payload.body:
So when I created the original PR, it wasn't on a per-track basis but a per-album basis i.e. you had to take or leave the entire new album. That meant it was only useful when you had it comparing automatically because when you were interactive, you could already choose to upgrade or leave it based on the bitrate comparison beets already shows you.

That's actually less relevant to your PR now that I think about it. We should probably add the option to the interactive part too.

payload.author: semohr
payload.body:
Hi!

It would have been nice and transparent to disclose that you're also the author of `lrcmux`.

Since the project is still very new (it's only a few days old), I would prefer to postpone both this PR and any upstream integration into beets until the project has had more time to mature. At this stage, it's difficult to assess its long-term viability and whether it will see continued development and maintenance. We tend to be fairly conservative about adding new integrations because we will be responsible for maintaining them going forward.

This isn't a criticism of you or your project. I'm generally in favor of adding useful new functionality, but as things stand today, integrating `lrcmux` into upstream feels a bit premature. We wouldd be happy to revisit this once the project has had some time to settle in tho.

payload.author: Serene-Arc
payload.body:
I agree with @semohr and would also add that adding `lrcmux` as a source for lyrics would, IMO, only be a good decision if the project is not only mature, but popular as an aggregate service among beets users. Even if it remains updated and matures, it's still a service that adds an intermediary layer to other APIs.

I can see the usefulness as a user that doesn't want to go to a number of sites to get lyrics, but we provide a tool ourselves. I think there would have to be a compelling case to use `lrcmux` rather than just implementing the same API handling that it possesses ourselves. Otherwise it feels like adding an unnecessary intermediary to the process. There are five providers that `lrcmux` uses and we already actually integrate two of the five used, plus some others beside.

I think there would have to be compelling case to use this rather than simply implementing the Kugou, NetEase, and YouTube Music interfaces ourselves. Then at least we would own the code and be able to test and manage it thoroughly.

payload.author: f1nniboy
payload.body:
Fair points, and I understand the "we should just do it ourselves instead of relying on a central point of failure". But:

Of the common providers (Genius, LRCLIB, Musixmatch), only LRCLIB actually works out of the box right now. The bundled Genius API key is rate-limited and quite over its daily limit, one issue with using a central API key for such a big project. Musixmatch+Tekstowo have been off by default. And the Google search backend needs an API key supplied by the user. So realistically a regular setup fetches from only LRCLIB, which definitely has alright track coverage, but nothing can beat fetching from many lyrics providers at once (and users actually need to submit lyrics).

On the "we can just implement YT Music/Kugou/etc. ourselves": I guess thats true, but these undocumented APIs will change over time and each breakage ends up being a beets issue to fix. That's kind of why I built lrcmux, so that not every music tool/app has to independently maintain the same set of scrapers. Fix once, and every user of the API benefits. It's really the tradeoff between directly owning the scraper code and maintenance burden.

On the "unnecessary intermediary" thing, there might actually be some benefits over doing it yourselves directly: shared cache across users (for not unnecessarily querying the upstream providers and providing fast results) and the operational side of it (dealing with blocks, scraping, rotation, etc.) already being handled. Musixmatch is blocked today, and e.g. even if you switched to the "lrcmux" approach for Musixmatch (not mine, to be fair), users would still get rate-limited regularly on their own IP.

If you don't trust the public instance or just want to host it yourself, you can easily do so (albeit with the drawback of encountering provider rate limits).

The PR would add lrcmux as one optional source, not the default. Users who want it could enable it, and the others can leave it disabled. I'm happy to maintain it here and keep it working if the API changes, that's obviously on me as the PR (and project) author.

(also, sorry about not disclosing that I'm the author 🫠)

payload.author: arsaboo
payload.body: I see both sides of the argument, and personally, I'm comfortable adding another lyrics provider if it helps expand what we support. At the moment, lrclib is essentially our only lyrics source. Any option that strengthens our coverage—particularly for Bollywood tracks—has my support. On top of that, it's a small pull request, so if LRCMux proves unreliable or fails to gain traction, we can drop it with little trouble.

payload.author: snejus
payload.body:
I agree with @arsaboo and @f1nniboy - we currently only have one reliable source left - `lrclib`. And even those requests are slow nowadays. I fetch lyrics a lot, so would be more than happy to try out a new provider, even if it's new and not yet proven.

Just rebase and fix the conflict in the changelog.

payload.author: f1nniboy
payload.body:
> @snejus Also add a test case to `test/plugins/lyrics_pages.py` to test fetching from `lrcmux`!

I'm not sure about this, as the lyrics results are non-deterministic (based on which provider responds first, at the same sync level) and as such the API response may change once the cached entry expires. So the test may fail in the future, even though the API still works fine. What do you think?

So the test may fail in the future, even though the API still works fine. What do you think?

Have a look at `TestLyricsSources`/`LyricsBackendTest`/`LyricsPluginMixin` in detail and you will find that we parametrize `LyricsPlugin` with the expected lyrics backend and set it in the plugin configuration. Thus, only `lrcmux` will be queried for that new test case.

payload.author: f1nniboy
payload.body:
> Another question we had: how does your API scale? Consider that once this is integrated into beets you will get many, many more requests compared to what you get now, I think.

Well, I haven't seen heavy API load in practice yet, but in theory it should scale pretty well. The entire API is stateless (it only needs Redis, maybe a DB in the future?), so I can just add more servers if the API itself ever struggles.

Proxy costs are negligible right now, and even projecting way up (10-20 requests/s) they're still small. I'm keeping an eye on traffic levels to scale up as needed.

And as popularity grows, the most popular tracks should be able to be served straight from cache.

> Have a look at `TestLyricsSources`/`LyricsBackendTest`/`LyricsPluginMixin` in detail and you will find that we parametrize `LyricsPlugin` with the expected lyrics backend and set it in the plugin configuration. Thus, only `lrcmux` will be queried for that new test case.
> 
> Just make sure that `lrcmux` backend is resolved correctly in `LyricsPage.source` and `LyricsPage.backend`.

Yeah, but the thing is, the lrcmux API itself will return different providers' results (each provider has slightly different lyrics for that song) depending on latency if it has to query providers again (after the cache expires), so the expected .lrc response in the test may not match what the API actually returns in the future. I wanted to avoid having a hardcoded provider order to optimize for speed.

payload.author: snejus
payload.body:
> Yeah, but the thing is, the lrcmux API itself will return different providers' results (each provider has slightly different lyrics for that song) depending on latency if it has to query providers again (after the cache expires), so the expected .lrc response in the test may not match what the API actually returns in the future. I wanted to avoid having a hardcoded provider order to optimize for speed.

Ah, that's not ideal. Did you see the logic I added for `lrclib`?

payload.author: f1nniboy
payload.body:
> Ah, that's not ideal. Did you see the logic I added for `lrclib`?

You mean fetching LRCLIB lyrics by ID? That would work for the test, but in the actual search() I would still want to keep the title+artist+duration+album query parameters, which wouldn't work with the test. I could add a `sources` parameter of some sort to the API to control which providers to use, but then I would also have to add `lrcmux_sources` as a config option. Should I do that?

payload.author: snejus
payload.body:
> but then I would also have to add `lrcmux_sources` as a config option. Should I do that?

Maybe no need in such case. We still somehow want to prove that 'hey, this provider still works' in the test. The worry I have is more related to using the plugin. For example, if I fetch synchronised lyrics from `lrcmux`, and then refetch them later, does it mean that I may end up with different lyrics later?

payload.author: f1nniboy
payload.body: Well, it depends. Right now I cache fetched lyrics for up to a year (maybe a permanent DB in the future), and after that, if you try to fetch them again, it will go through the entire provider fetching thing again, where the fastest (and highest sync level) provider wins. Providers could also be down temporarily/rate-limited/failed/whatever when you refetch. So it could be Musixmatch again, but you may also get lyrics from Kugou, etc. These lyrics shouldn't be *that* different from eachother, and you shouldn't get wrong lyrics either way. The only way to get the same lyrics again is setting the `sources` parameter to one provider only.

payload.author: snejus
payload.body: Sounds good to me!

payload.author: snejus
payload.body:
And... I changed my mind regarding the test - just realised that `lrcmux.sources` is indeed a configuration option. Please do add an autouse fixture that sets one specific source in `lrcmux.sources` when `backend == "lrcmux"` and add a test case please! 

Note that these tests are run only when `lyrics` plugin contents have changed, so you won't get ddosed here 😅

payload.author: arnavahire19
payload.body:
@semohr 
So, we decided to ditch the old way of building queries by scraping every track's metadata and switched to just using the artist/album info Beets gives us. Here’s why:

 **Fixes Manual Searches:** Before, when you’d manually fix tags during an import, the plugin ignored you and just re-ran the original (wrong) search. Now, it actually uses your input.
 **Way More Efficient:** The old `_album_queries` was creating a massive mess of redundant API calls to Tidal every time tags were inconsistent. Now it’s just one clean query per search.

### The TL;DR:

**Behavioral:** Manual searches now actually work like they're suppose to.
**Performance:** Way fewer API calls, so you won't hit Tidal's rate limits as much.
 **Consistency:** Keeps the code in line with the major plugins like Beatport and Deezer.

payload.author: semohr
payload.body:
> Way More Efficient: The old _album_queries was creating a massive mess of redundant API calls to Tidal every time tags were inconsistent. Now it’s just one clean query per search.

We actually use multiple queries because the Tidal API doesn’t handle search terms very well. The extra overhead is intentional and improves result quality significantly. I also intentionally sidestepped the majority vote logic for artist and title here for the same reason.

> Consistency: Keeps the code in line with the major plugins like Beatport and Deezer.

Tidal is the newest plugin and in my opinion one of the cleanest metadata plugin implementations in beets. We should not try to compare it to the `Beatport` and `Deezer` plugin too much. These are probably the least maintained ones in beets. The beatport plugin is even deprecated and will likely be removed in 3.0.0.

---

@snejus Input wanted:

At the moment there’s no clean plugin-level way to distinguish whether album or artist strings originate from user input versus being inferred (see [`tag_album` function](https://github.com/beetbox/beets/blob/08081f3c440c3aff2ff66931af645c92edfceb47/beets/autotag/match.py#L383)).

That effectively forces us into using `likelies` (majority vote) for artists and titles. However, this reduces tidal match quality because it discards valid alternative interpretations too early.

I’d prefer to keep the more verbose multi-query approach since it improves search results. Any ideas on how to better surface "user intent vs inferred metadata" without breaking the existing plugins? (Was thinking e.g. changing the `candidates` signature could work)

payload.author: arnavahire19
payload.body:
Thanks for the explanation, @semohr! That makes complete sense. I appreciate the context on     
  Tidal's search API behavior and why the multi-query approach is necessary for match quality      
  there, as well as the heads-up regarding Beatport/Deezer plugin maintenance status.              
                                                                                                   
  Regarding the architectural challenge of distinguishing user-initiated manual search from        
  automatic/inferred tag search at the plugin level:                                               
                                                                                                   
  Here are two backwards-compatible ways we could implement this without breaking existing plugins:
                                                                                                   
  #### Option 1: Optional Keyword Argument + Introspection (Recommended)                           
                                                                                                   
  We can update the core plugin runner to pass an optional keyword argument (e.g.,  user_initiated:
  bool = False ) to  candidates  and  item_candidates .                                            
                                                                                                   
  To prevent breaking third-party or older plugins that don't accept this argument, the core hook  
  caller can inspect the signature of the plugin's  candidates  method:                            
                                                                                                   
    import inspect                                                                                 
                                                                                                   
    # Inside beets core hook dispatch:                                                             
    sig = inspect.signature(plugin.candidates)                                                     
    kwargs = {}                                                                                    
    if 'user_initiated' in sig.parameters:                                                         
        kwargs['user_initiated'] = is_manual_search  # determined by importer state                
                                                                                                   
    plugin.candidates(items, artist, album, va_likely, **kwargs)                                   
                                                                                                   
  This allows the Tidal plugin (and any future plugins) to opt-in by simply adding  user_initiated:
  bool = False  to their signatures. When  True  (e.g., user manually entered search terms), the   
  plugin can trust the input and skip redundant fallback queries. When  False  (automatic imports),
  it can execute the fallback multi-query logic.                                                   
                                                                                                   
  #### Option 2: Add a Context Object                                                              
                                                                                                   
  Instead of changing method signatures, we could pass an optional context dictionary or object    
  containing query metadata:                                                                       
                                                                                                   
    def candidates(                                                                                
        self, items: Sequence[Item], artist: str, album: str, va_likely: bool, context:            
  QueryContext | None = None

payload.body:
> Here are two backwards-compatible ways we could implement this without breaking existing plugins:

We can ask an LLM for ideas ourselves... Please don't paste LLM-generated design suggestions into the review and present them as your proposals. It's not particularly helpful to the discussion and doesn't move the design forward in any meaningful way unless you've evaluated and argued for the approach yourself.

More importantly, none of this should be implemented in this PR. These changes are well outside the scope of the issue, and the proper integration and design need considerably more thought and discussion first.

Thanks for already taking a look here!

We should be able to resolve all search limit based logic within the `candidates` and  `item_candidates` function. I don't really see the need for the extensive drilling. 

The `search_tracks_by_query` and `search_albums_by_query` functions are returning iterators. We should be able to break them early and limit the number of requests that way. 

Additionally the `search_limit` currently does not respect the  `_album_queries` and `_item_queries` loop. We might want to have a round robin approach here.

---

I will have a more detailed look next week.

payload.author: JOJ0
payload.body:
Hi @semohr appologies for not responding earlier. I'm already picturing how useful the new default mode will be:

>     This mode explains what beets is doing in a more explicit way than
>     ``legacy``, including key decisions such as matching, tagging, and
>     file operations, without exposing full internal debug information.

This sounds promising and exactly what I'm often missing in beets. More info, less noise!

What I can't grasp is how this would look like from a plugin developer's perspective. Would we still simply write a log line that looks like this: `self._log.info("...", arg)`? Would we still only have to define "one explicit log level" for a message? Or would we have to define which log level and as well in which mode it is displayed?


Also I'm wondering if this feature wish could be realised (without using grep): Display regular output of `beets plugincmd` and give me DEBUG level of only _plugincmd_, not the other plugins and not core DEBUG stuff. 

Maybe all dumb questions but some example snippets of how calls would look like and how refactoring of existing log calls could look like (if required). Many thanks for this proposal!

payload.author: semohr
payload.body:
Thanks for having a look! You think anything of the following should go into the docs?

---

> What I can't grasp is how this would look like from a plugin developer's perspective. Would we still simply write a log line that looks like this: self._log.info("...", arg)? Would we still only have to define "one explicit log level" for a message? Or would we have to define which log level and as well in which mode it is displayed?

Things should not change from a plugin developer's perspective. You would continue to use the existing logging API, for example:
```
self._log.info("Info message")
self._log.debug("Info message")
self._log.warning("Info message")
# Or equivalently:
logging.getLogger("beets.<plugin>").info("info message")
```

Plugin developers would still only choose the appropriate log level (info, debug, warning, etc.). The new modes do not introduce an additional concept that plugins need to target. Instead, they determine which log messages are shown in the terminal and how they are presented. In other words, the modes are simply an abstraction over the logging configuration.

---

> Also I'm wondering if this feature wish could be realised (without using grep): Display regular output of beets plugincmd and give me DEBUG level of only plugincmd, not the other plugins and not core DEBUG stuff.

Yes, that should be possible if we decide to allow custom modes. Personally, my ideal configuration would be to only show `warning` and `error` messages in the console, while writing everything else (including debug output) to a log file. But that's just my personal preference. :)

---

> Maybe all dumb questions but some example snippets of how calls would look like and how refactoring of existing log calls could look like (if required). Many thanks for this proposal!

The dump questions are the ones not asked :upside_down_face: Modes can simply be thought of as predefined logging configurations that a user can toggle. The concept does not really propagate into the code beyond the initial logging configuration. From a plugin maintainer's perspective, there should be no refactoring required.

payload.author: JOJ0
payload.body: Love the log file idea! I'm missing this since ever! ❤️

payload.author: Serene-Arc
payload.body:
Couple things. First, is it worth having all these additional configuration options when the standard is `-v` flags for command-line interfaces? It seems like a lot of extra stuff. Those built-in modes correlate exactly with increasing levels of `-v`.

Also, one thing that I've done for a project with lots of diagnostic output that normal users aren't really interested in is, by default, have a logging file with the maximum level of information by default. It's written to with each run of the program and as part of bug reports, we can just point users to that and have it pasted in the report. It might simplify things in that respect.

We should definitely be using the built-in logging features that Python comes with more. Being able to specify those through the YAML is a nice touch.

payload.author: semohr
payload.body:
Thanks for having a look and the reply! Here my thought, hope it gives you insights into my perspective :)

---

> Couple things. First, is it worth having all these additional configuration options when the standard is -v flags for command-line interfaces? It seems like a lot of extra stuff. Those built-in modes correlate exactly with increasing levels of -v.

From my perspective, beets has always stood out because of how customizable and configurable it is. In the same way giving users the freedom to configure the logging freely opens up genuinely useful new avenues.

Regarding the verbose options it is intended to correlate with the logging modes (it already mostly behaves the way I have written up in the specs). Verbosity adjusts the level of what gets logged, while the mode controls the initial configuration, like formatting, handlers, colors, all that stuff. 

In that regard `modes` and `verbose` options seem orthogonal to me. I imagine I would set a mode (which I like and maybe even customized) as default in the config file and than adjust the level with the `-v` flag if I need more information. Ofc one can also use `--logging` as that is our common interface for configuration options. I see this cli argument mostly used when reporting issues (with `--logging debug`) or maybe depending on a user workflows.

> Also, one thing that I've done for a project with lots of diagnostic output that normal users aren't really interested in is, by default, have a logging file with the maximum level of information by default. It's written to with each run of the program and as part of bug reports, we can just point users to that and have it pasted in the report. It might simplify things in that respect.

I was thinking about this but I don't want to enforce it for the same reason as above. Imo beets tries to be a agnostic framework and should not lock people into a singular opinion. MAX level is also not too well defined: does it include DEBUG from third-party libraries? From plugins? What about tracing information? 

There seem to be many subjective takes here. Instead of baking in one opinionated default, different modes and the escapehatch with arbitrary logging configs lets us stay impartial.

payload.author: semohr
payload.body:
> High-level impact: this reduces duplicated type definitions, makes the shared contract clearer, and simplifies future changes to common Tidal metadata without changing album- and track-specific types.


I disagree with this point. While this reduces duplication, I think it makes future API changes harder to reason about because the types no longer align directly with the TIDAL contract. When the API changes, it's no longer sufficient to compare a resource definition against its corresponding type; instead, you need to trace shared fields through an additional abstraction layer. That indirection makes it more difficult to validate that our types still faithfully represent the upstream API. If the TIDAL API ever diverges between albums and tracks, I'll happily dust off this comment and collect my "I told you so" points :rofl:

payload.author: semohr
payload.body:
Hi, and thanks for the PR.

In the discussion, I asked about the motivation and intended use cases for this plugin, but I don't think we've fully explored that yet.

As it stands, I'm struggling to understand why this functionality should be introduced as a dedicated plugin in beets. The proposed workflow appears to be something that can already be implemented using the existing [hooks](https://docs.beets.io/en/latest/plugins/hook.html) plugin and external tooling.

Could you elaborate on the points raised in the discussion?

Understanding the reasoning and intended workflow would help us evaluate whether this is something that belongs in beets itself, or whether it is better served through existing extension mechanisms.

---

Separately, regardless of the outcome of that discussion, the implementation will need to conform to our coding and contribution standards. Please take a look at the contribution guide here: https://docs.beets.io/en/latest/contributing.html.

payload.author: semohr
payload.body:
> We are not currently exposing popularity information in UI. This is mostly for the DB so that we can use it for other smart things (playlists)

I mean the query syntax with UX. The question is whether users should have separate fields per entity, such as:
```bash
beet ls tidal_album_popularity:5..20
```
or a single generic field whose meaning depends on the search scope, for example:
```
beet ls tidal_popularity:5..50 -a
```
The latter is shorter and more flexible, but the former is more explicit and consistent across entity types.

payload.author: semohr
payload.body:
Thanks! It's great to see more activity around the TIDAL plugin. I already did a quick scan of the changes, but I'll do a more thorough review next week.

---

I think we should keep the requested capabilities (`scope`) out of the user configuration. While I understand it's convenient to make this configurable during development, I can foresee quite a few user errors if it's exposed.

I see two possible approaches:

* Run the TIDAL plugin with `search.read user.read` by default.
* Run with only `search.read` by default, and automatically request `user.read` when the `tidal lyrics` plugin is enabled.

I'd vote for the first option. It keeps the configuration simpler and avoids potential issues for users. The `user.read` scope will be needed at some point anyways if we want e.g. to allow users to use their own music.

@snejus Any strong opinion here?

payload.author: treyturner

The `user.read` scope was my misunderstanding that we'd get the same data back from the v2 API as I got from the legacy `r_usr` scope on the v1 API, but this seems to not be the case. I can't actually get the v2 API to hand me lyrics with any scope I'm able to configure at the moment, so I'm going to cut this back over to the v1 API totally independent of the built-in `tidal` plugin and will release it as an external plugin. I was too eager to contribute to `tidal` once I saw it existed and didn't identify the risk of functional gaps in the API version change since the documentation suggests they're still retrievable.

I'm really sad it can't land in the project and want to apologize again for the hassle. If I see something change in the API I'll pick it back up; I was also hoping to add Tidal as an art source.

payload.author: semohr
payload.body:
I might be misunderstanding the intended workflow here. Even after reading the documentation, the PR description, and the code itself, I'm still not entirely sure what the intended use case is.

Couldn't duplicate resolution happen as a separate step in the pipeline after a match has been chosen? That would align better with my mental model, since we'd be working with the normalized metadata rather than the "raw" tags. Track and album level de-duplication should happen depending on the chosen candidate not the audios metadata imo.

I understand that the duplicate check is currently performed before autotagging, but I'm struggling to see what advantages that provides over doing it afterward.



---

Could we clearly define the intended behavior and use case at a high level. Having an abstract description of the workflow and its goals would make it much easier to reason about whether the current implementation is the right approach.

payload.author: tommyschnabel
payload.body:
Hey @semohr thanks for the review! I'm pretty new to this repo still, and so I'm really relying on your and @snejus's architectural suggestions. Making this a new step really makes sense, let me look into doing that. For reference, I had an earlier PR adding this check to the `duplicates` plugin, which @snejus helpfully pointed out would belong better in the main import code, so that's how we got here.

As a general point, it's rarely wanted behavior to import the same track multiple times, and obviously deduping is the way to stop this (my original use-case was re-importing a whole downloads dir multiple times before clearing it, and ending up with duplicates because of that). In my original implementation there was no concept of deduping albums; I was specifically targeting the track level only, and only looking at the album as a whole if it becomes empty due to skipping dedupes. 

So that brings me to the high level behavior of: 
**1. when an incoming track has a matching track in the db, we apply the config setting for deduping (keep, skip, remove, ask)
2. if all tracks from an album import are skipped, the album is also skipped**

I really do appreciate the reviews and the pointers on how you guys want this organized. Again, I'm very new to the repo and am happy to change whatever to help see this feature through.

payload.author: semohr
payload.body:
Alright that clears things up a bit for me.

> 1. when an incoming track has a matching track in the db, we apply the config setting for deduping (keep, skip, remove, ask)

What do you mean by incoming track? In general, I would avoid using `items` for this use case and instead operate on `candidates`, since they already contain the processed and normalized metadata. This is also how album-level deduplication works: we operate on matched candidates, and if we detect duplicates for any retrieved candidate, we mark it accordingly and let the user decide how to proceed.

I would approach track-level deduplication in the same way for consistency and unification.

> 2. if all tracks from an album import are skipped, the album is also skipped

I would fold this into a single decision point for the user (config-based behavior also possible). From the UI layer perspective, I would expect something like this:

```
Duplicates detected:

Album-level duplicate:
  • Actions available: Skip | Merge | Keep old | Replace with new

Track-level duplicates (found x duplicates out of y):
  • Actions available: Skip | Merge | Keep old | Replace with new | Select per track
```

---

We haven't really but this in the docs yet but if you need a primer on the notations and different parts of the matching flows have a look here: https://github.com/beetbox/beets/issues/6683

BTW I didn't give this a proper review but realize looking at diffs passing by that there is quite verbose commenting (possibly agent-generated). So a general note/advice: Comments in complex areas like this are useful and appreciated but try to reduce them to a minimum. For example here the comment is redundant. The simple code and log message tells that same story already:


```
+        if config["import"]["quiet"]:
+            # In quiet mode, don't prompt -- just skip the duplicate tracks.
+            log.info("Skipping duplicate tracks.")
+            return dict.fromkeys(track_duplicates, DuplicateAction.SKIP)
```

Or alternatively, which is also less distracting in my opinion: Move code explanations you find useful to the docstring.

payload.author: snejus
payload.body:
Thanks for the PR. I’m going to close this because the crash comes from an unsupported dependency state rather than a beets bug.

Current `pyproject.toml` requires `requests >=2.32.5`, and supported Requests versions expose the JSON decode exception used by the lyrics plugin. The traceback in #5998 shows beets loading `requests` from the system site packages, which is older than the version beets declares support for.

The right fix is to update the installation environment so beets runs with a supported Requests version, for example by upgrading `requests` or installing beets in a clean virtual environment. I don’t think we should add compatibility code for dependency versions outside the package contract.

payload.author: holy-elbow
payload.title: POC lyrics to txt

payload.author: snejus
payload.body:
Thanks for the PR. I think the feature could be useful, but this implementation currently introduces a couple of crash paths that need to be addressed before it can move forward.

The main blocker is that the new writer runs unconditionally whenever lyrics are updated. The default config sets `write_to_file.directory` to `None`, so a normal `beet lyrics` run now reaches `Path(self.directory)` and raises a `TypeError` even when the user has not enabled txt output. This should be gated behind an explicit config value so the existing lyrics workflow remains unchanged by default.

There is also an issue with the `album_folder` mode. beets stores `Item.path` as bytes, but `Path(item.path)` does not accept bytes paths. This should use `item.filepath` instead.

Also, why are you using `LyricsRequestsHandler` for writing?

One behavior question: should this only write files when new lyrics are fetched, or should it also be able to export lyrics that are already present in the library? The current early return for existing lyrics means it only works as a fetch-time side effect. That may be fine, but I think it should be intentional and covered by tests.

Could you add focused tests for the disabled-by-default case and the `album_folder` path handling? Also, CI issues need to be addressed.

payload.author: holy-elbow
payload.body:
> Thanks for the PR. I think the feature could be useful, but this implementation currently introduces a couple of crash paths that need to be addressed before it can move forward.
> 
> The main blocker is that the new writer runs unconditionally whenever lyrics are updated. The default config sets `write_to_file.directory` to `None`, so a normal `beet lyrics` run now reaches `Path(self.directory)` and raises a `TypeError` even when the user has not enabled txt output. This should be gated behind an explicit config value so the existing lyrics workflow remains unchanged by default.
> 
> There is also an issue with the `album_folder` mode. beets stores `Item.path` as bytes, but `Path(item.path)` does not accept bytes paths. This should use `item.filepath` instead.
> 
> Also, why are you using `LyricsRequestsHandler` for writing?
> 
> One behavior question: should this only write files when new lyrics are fetched, or should it also be able to export lyrics that are already present in the library? The current early return for existing lyrics means it only works as a fetch-time side effect. That may be fine, but I think it should be intentional and covered by tests.
> 
> Could you add focused tests for the disabled-by-default case and the `album_folder` path handling? Also, CI issues need to be addressed.

Hi, thank you for the quick reply! This is my first time not just contributing to beets, but working on the code base at all. This is a feature I have wanted for some time and decided to finally give it a shot. I skimmed through the existing code and did my best to emulate the formatting, as for calling LyricsRequestHandler, I copied the basic init structure of the Translator class and included it just to be safe as I wasnt fully certain if it was needed or not for what I was trying to accomplish.

I have already been using a hack way to create lyric files from the database by printing them to stdout and piping it into a file. I am sure I can come up with a more elegant solution to work inside of the lyrics plugin, as ideally I want to add the option for people who have pre-existing databases and want to quickly generate the files. 

Ive pushed an update to my code (hopefully) fixing the issues. I should have time next week to put a bunch of time into testing and fixing any remaining issues.

> Just had a short look. Could you give a more specific reasoning why we need this? Is it needed for changes we have planned or simplifies them?

I was adding types to `beets.importer` module and ended up having to make `FormattedMapping` inherit from `Mapping` (as the TODO above outlines as well):

```diff

 fd121d626c7a23244fd69bb177f56fe43fa30f8a 
 2026-05-30 18:02 / Šarūnas Nejus <snejus@protonmail.com>
 2026-05-31 08:23 / Šarūnas Nejus <snejus@protonmail.com>
 
    
    Add missing types to importer.tasks



diff --git a/beets/dbcore/db.py b/beets/dbcore/db.py
index cc882eae5..b988211d7 100755
--- a/beets/dbcore/db.py
+++ b/beets/dbcore/db.py
@@ -171,23 +171,23 @@ def _get_formatted
 
 
 # NOTE: This seems like it should be a `Mapping`, i.e.
 # ```
 # class LazyConvertDict(Mapping[str, Any])
 # ```
 # but there are some conflicts with the `Mapping` protocol such that we
 # can't do this without changing behaviour: In particular, iterators returned
 # by some methods build intermediate lists, such that modification of the
 # `LazyConvertDict` becomes safe during iteration. Some code does in fact rely
 # on this.
-class LazyConvertDict:
+class LazyConvertDict(Mapping[str, Any]):
     """Set the base data that should be lazily converted"""
```

beets/dbcore/db.py:222: error: Return type "list[str]" of "keys" incompatible with return type "KeysView[str]" in supertype "typing.Mapping"  [override]
beets/dbcore/db.py:240: error: Return type "Iterable[tuple[str, Any]]" of "items" incompatible with return type "ItemsView[str, Any]" in supertype "typing.Mapping"  [override]
Found 2 errors in 1 file (checked 1 source file)
```

payload.author: copilot-pull-request-reviewer
payload.body:
## Pull request overview

grug look at PR. PR move `Match`, `AlbumMatch`, `TrackMatch` from `beets.autotag.hooks` into `beets.autotag.match`, and make `beets.autotag` package the one tidy front door for everything: `Distance`, `Info`, `Match`, `assign_items`, `tag_album`, `tag_item`, friends. All caller code, plugin code, tests, doc snippet updated to import from `beets.autotag`. grug like — less reach into deep module, complexity demon get smaller pantry.

Only one rock in path: `test/autotag/test_hooks.py` import `AttrDict` from `beets.autotag`, but `beets/autotag/__init__.py` never re-export `AttrDict` and not list in `__all__`. Package `__getattr__` will raise `AttributeError`, so test collection will break.

**Changes:**
- Move `Match`/`AlbumMatch`/`TrackMatch` (and their imports of `plugins`, `dataclass`) from `hooks.py` into `match.py`; tighten `hooks.py` runtime imports
- Expand `beets/autotag/__init__.py` re-exports and `__all__`; drop the `Distance` deprecation redirect
- Rewrite every internal/plugin/test/doc import to use the flat `beets.autotag` API

### Reviewed changes

Copilot reviewed 37 out of 37 changed files in this pull request and generated 1 comment.

<details>
<summary>Show a summary per file</summary>

| File | Description |
| ---- | ----------- |
| beets/autotag/__init__.py | Re-export distance/hooks/match public names, drop `Distance` deprecation entry |
| beets/autotag/hooks.py | Remove `Match`/`AlbumMatch`/`TrackMatch` and now-unused `plugins`, `dataclass`, `TYPE_CHECKING` imports |
| beets/autotag/match.py | New home for `Match`/`AlbumMatch`/`TrackMatch`; move `Proposal` below them; type-only imports for `Info`/`AlbumInfo`/`TrackInfo`/`Distance`/`Album`/`Item`/`JSONDict`/`AnyMatch`/`Candidates` |
